An epithet is a word or short phrase that is attached to — or used in place of — a person's or thing's actual name, in order to describe or highlight a specific quality about them.

Think of it as a label that sticks. It captures something essential, memorable, or defining about whoever or whatever it's describing.
The Three Main Ways "Epithet" is Used

The word "epithet" carries three closely related but distinct senses. Understanding all three will prepare you for any context in which you encounter it.

1. A Descriptive Title or Nickname Attached to a Name

This is the broadest and most fundamental sense. An epithet is a characterizing word or phrase placed alongside someone's name — often to celebrate, honor, or permanently define them by one of their qualities.

Examples:

  • "Alexander the Great" — "the Great" is the epithet. It describes his extraordinary military achievements and attaches permanently to his name.
  • "Ivan the Terrible" — "the Terrible" is the epithet. It captures the fearsome, brutal quality of his reign.
  • "Richard the Lionheart" — "the Lionheart" is the epithet. It paints him as brave and fierce.
  • "God Almighty" — "Almighty" is the epithet. It highlights omnipotence.

Notice the pattern: the actual name stays (Alexander, Ivan, Richard), and the epithet rides alongside it as a descriptive badge.

Epithets used this way can be positive, neutral, or negative. They just pin a defining quality to a name.

2. A Literary / Poetic Epithet (Especially in Epic Poetry)

In literature, an epithet is a fixed, repeated descriptive phrase that a writer pairs consistently with a particular name or subject across a work. These are sometimes called "Homeric epithets" because the ancient Greek poet Homer used them masterfully and frequently in works like The Iliad and The Odyssey.

Examples from Homer:

  • "swift-footed Achilles" — Achilles is almost always called this, even when he isn't running. "Swift-footed" is his epithet.
  • "grey-eyed Athena" — Athena is consistently described this way.
  • "rosy-fingered Dawn" — Every time the sun rises in Homer, Dawn gets this same epithet.
  • "the wine-dark sea" — The sea is repeatedly called this.

Why use fixed, repeating phrases? In ancient oral poetry, which was spoken and memorized rather than written, these set phrases helped the poet (and the audience) keep track of characters and gave the poetry a pleasing rhythm. But the practice spread well beyond Homer.

Modern literary epithets work similarly — a writer gives a character or place a recurring descriptive tag:

  • "the old man" (a character consistently referred to this way rather than by name)
  • "the city of light" (a fixed poetic name for Paris)

The key feature of a literary epithet is its repeatability and consistency — it is used again and again, almost like a refrain, to evoke the same quality each time.

3. An Abusive or Offensive Term (The Modern Everyday Sense)

This is the sense you are most likely to encounter in modern newspapers, conversations, and everyday life. In this sense, an epithet is an insulting, derogatory, or hateful word used to attack or demean a person or group, typically based on their race, religion, gender, nationality, sexuality, or other identity.

When people say "racial epithet," "hurled an epithet," or "a slur," they are using this sense of the word.

Examples in context:

  • "The suspect was charged after shouting racial epithets at the victim."
  • "The comment section was filled with hateful epithets."
  • "She was deeply hurt by the epithet used against her."

In this sense, the epithet is not just a description — it is a weapon of language. It reduces a person to something negative, stereotyped, or contemptible.

Why does this sense exist? It connects logically to the first sense. An epithet is already a label that defines someone. When that label is hostile and meant to wound rather than describe neutrally, it becomes an insult — an abusive epithet.
How to Know Which Sense Is Meant

Context almost always makes this clear:

Clue in the sentenceLikely sense
A name followed by a title-like phrase ("the Great," "the Wise")Descriptive title / nickname
Discussion of epic poetry, Homer, literature, or recurring phrasesLiterary / poetic epithet
Words like "racial," "hateful," "hurled," "slur," or a social contextAbusive / offensive epithet

To put it plainly:

  • If someone is "Alexander the Great," the epithet honors him.
  • If Homer calls Achilles "swift-footed Achilles" repeatedly, the epithet is a literary device.
  • If someone shouts a slur at a stranger, that slur is an epithet in the abusive sense.

Despite their differences in tone and context, all three uses of "epithet" share the same DNA:

An epithet is a word or phrase that characterizes someone or something by pinning a quality to their name or identity.

Whether that quality is glorious ("the Great"), poetic ("swift-footed"), or hateful (a slur) — the mechanism is the same. A label is attached. A quality is highlighted. The name and the description become inseparable in the mind of the reader or listener.
A Quick Contrast to Avoid Confusion

An epithet is not quite the same as:

  • A metaphor — a metaphor compares one thing to another ("He is a lion"). An epithet tags a quality directly onto a name ("Richard the Lionheart").
  • A nickname — a nickname can be entirely arbitrary or affectionate ("Buddy," "Skip"). An epithet always describes or characterizes something meaningful.
  • A title (like "Doctor" or "Sir") — these indicate rank or profession, not a personal defining quality.

An epithet is a descriptive word or phrase that gets attached to a name or used in its place, in order to highlight a defining quality of a person, place, or thing. It can be a historical nickname that sticks to someone forever ("Ivan the Terrible"), a repeated poetic phrase in literature ("grey-eyed Athena"), or — in its most common modern use — a hateful slur hurled at a person to demean them. In all cases, the epithet is a characterizing label: it takes one quality and stamps it onto an identity, sometimes to honor, sometimes to paint a picture, and sometimes to harm.
